scenario: AITA for insisting my daughter get a job even though we don't need her rent? | My 23 year old daughter Kirsty (not real name of course) lost her job in the city after testing positive for drugs. Kirsty was and is devastated and hasn't been doing much except crying in her room and going out clubbing with her friends. She has been like this for three months. and is starting to run low on money. Given that she has no chance of getting back into her career, I've been encouraging her to try to find some entry level work like retail/shop work or something like that. She sees it as a ''waste of her talents'' and thinks she's worth more than that. We have been arguing about it a lot. My wife Sarah and I don't need the rent from her, but at the same time she's been sitting here doing nothing for three months and asking for money from us. I told her that if she didn't make the effort to find another job she would have to find alternative living arrangements and she ran off crying. Sarah is mad at me. She agrees that working a job like that is a waste of Kirsty's ability. She did very well academically and was headhunted by her company as soon as she graduated. She had even been promoted to assistant manager not long before being sacked. Sarah had a go at me, saying that it wasn't fair for me to ''threaten'' her into getting a job that isn't good enough for her even though we don't need her rent money. I think I did the right thing. Happy to be a shoulder to cry on about the loss of her career, but not willing to let her spend the rest of her life living of us.

This intentional reflection can lead to a deeper understanding of the consequences of their mistakes and a stronger motivation to make amends and change their behavior. Having a dedicated day for introspection can also help individuals develop a greater sense of self-awareness, which can, in turn, influence their decision-making and behavior throughout the year. By regularly examining their actions and their impact on others, individuals may become more mindful of the potential consequences of their choices and more inclined to consider the well-being of those around them. This can lead to a greater willingness to apologize, make amends, and learn from mistakes, rather than trying to justify or deny them. By acknowledging and accepting their mistakes, individuals can develop a more growth-oriented mindset, which can help them approach challenges and setbacks with a greater sense of resilience and determination. It's also worth noting that the act of seeking forgiveness and making amends can have a profound impact on relationships and personal growth. By taking responsibility for past wrongs and working to repair harm, individuals can strengthen their connections with others, rebuild trust, and develop a greater sense of empathy and compassion. Overall, having a day like Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously one takes their mistakes and can have a lasting impact on personal growth, relationships, and overall well-being.
